method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity' (published 26 February 2021), 15 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC7969540). S2: QUOTED from Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review) 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management' (published 10 July 2025), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12245930). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim (S1, IAB consensus 2021) unchanged and adds S2, a 2025 UK narrative review of hemifacial spasm, because no Australian source and no open, current hemifacial spasm guideline or consensus was found (Europe PMC searches 2026-09-24: hemifacial spasm or blepharospasm with guideline/consensus/recommendation in the title, 2018-2026; blepharospasm or hemifacial spasm with Australia and consensus or guideline; hemifacial spasm reviews 2020-2026).

claims.claim: **Botulinum toxin therapy is individual: hit the right muscle with the right dose.** Both are recorded in an injection scheme, which may take several injection series to optimise.
claims.source_text: The basic principle of BT therapy for motor indications is to select the appropriate target muscles and to apply appropriate BT doses to them, or in short: 'Hit the right muscle with the right dose'. These two aspects are documented in the injection scheme. The development of the injection scheme is based on knowledge and experience, and will be highly individualised for each patient treated. It may require several subsequent injection series to be optimised.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Choose target muscles by documenting the abnormal posture and movements**, and tell compensatory or protective muscle activity apart from the primary abnormal activity.
claims.source_text: Target muscles are selected by documentation of the patient's pathological positioning and movements. Based on the understanding of physiological muscle functioning, pathologically active muscles are identified. Muscle pain may contribute to additional information. Compensatory muscle activity and protective postures have to be identified and need to be distinguished from primary pathological muscle activity.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use the lowest dose that gives a robust, lasting effect.** Lower doses limit weakness, spread to neighbouring muscles, total dose and cost. The dose depends on muscle mass, the muscle's therapeutic window and the risk of weakening adjacent muscles.
claims.source_text: Only necessary BT doses should be applied. They should be as low as possible to reduce functional impairment, BT spread into adjacent muscles, excessive total doses and unnecessary costs. However, they should be high enough to produce robust and lasting therapeutic effects. Dosing depends on the target muscle's mass, its therapeutic window and the paresis risk in adjacent muscles.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adjust within the dose range:** go higher when abnormal activity is strong and helper muscles are available, lower when the abnormal activity is functionally useful (as in dystonic tremor).
claims.source_text: Individual BT dosing within these limits will be higher when the pathological muscle activity is high and when supportive agonistic muscles are available. BT doses will be lower when the pathological muscle activity is functionally useful, as in spasticity's paresis or in dystonic tremor
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Facial dystonia is the second most common dystonia.** In the reference-centre series of 100 patients (mean age 65.2 years, 69% women), 45% also had cervical and 25% oromandibular dystonia.
claims.source_text: Facial dystonia is the second most common form of dystonia. In our group of 100 consecutive facial dystonia patients, their age was 65.2 ± 13.3 years and the sex ratio was 31% males and 69% females. 45% of these patients had additional cervical dystonia and 25% oromandibular dystonia.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Typical facial dose:** a total of 78.8 ± 31.6 MU (range 4 to 220 MU) across 3.7 ± 1.8 muscles. Orbicularis oculi (pars orbitalis) was injected in 91%, procerus in 32% and orbicularis oculi (pars palpebralis) in 26%.
claims.source_text: The total facial BT dose was 78.8 ± 31.6 MU (minimum 4 MU, maximum 220 MU). The number of target muscles was 3.7 ± 1.8 (minimum 1, maximum 10). Most frequently used target muscles were M. orbicularis oculi/Pars orbitalis (91%), M. procerus (32%), M. orbicularis oculi/Pars palpebralis (26%)
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Injection cautions:** perioral injections readily cause weakness; inject frontalis carefully because it helps open the eyelid; add pars palpebralis of orbicularis oculi when there is an eyelid-opening apraxia component.
claims.source_text: BT injections into perioral muscles are prone to produce paretic adverse effects. The M. frontalis should be used carefully as it is an auxiliary eyelid opening muscle. The M. orbicularis oculi/Pars palpebralis is used when there is a component of eyelid opening apraxia.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hemifacial spasm (HFS) is involuntary, paroxysmal twitching of the facial-expression muscles on one side,** all supplied by that side's facial nerve. Women are affected about twice as often as men, onset is usually from the fourth to the sixth decade, and 2.6% of cases are bilateral.
claims.source_text: Hemifacial spasm (HFS) is a movement disorder characterized by involuntary, paroxysmal contractions of muscles involved in facial expression, which are innervated by the ipsilateral facial nerve. … with a 2:1 predilection for women over men … Disease onset usually occurs from the fourth through to the sixth decades of life … HFS is often sporadic and unilateral, but in 2.6% of cases may be bilateral
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The usual cause is a neurovascular conflict:** an ectatic or looping artery (typically the anterior- or posterior-inferior cerebellar artery or the vertebral artery) presses on the facial nerve in the posterior fossa.
claims.source_text: It is well established that an ectatic or aberrant arterial loop (typically the anterior-inferior cerebellar artery, posterior-inferior cerebellar artery, or vertebral artery) interacts with facial nerve fibers in the posterior fossa to induce HFS
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Image every patient with MRI** to exclude a structural cause (vestibular schwannoma, meningioma, arteriovenous anomaly); high-resolution T2 sequences with MRA can show the conflict. EEG and EMG help exclude mimics such as seizures and myokymia when the clinical signs are subtle.
claims.source_text: Investigations can be immensely helpful to exclude potential HFS mimics, particularly when the distinguishing clinical signs are absent or very subtle. … Electromyography (EMG) may also show short 5-150 Hz bursts of motor unit potentials, that appear as doublets, triplets or multiplets, to support a diagnosis of myokymia … Neuroimaging, in the form of MRI, remains invaluable to assess for potential structural causes, such as vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, or arteriovenous anomalies. … High-resolution T2-weighted sequences with MRA may also be able to demonstrate an area(s) of NVC
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A vessel touching the nerve is common without symptoms** (found on 38.8% of asymptomatic sides versus 97.9% of symptomatic ones), so the MRI needs a reader who knows facial-nerve root anatomy; first reports can miss the true compression or blame an incidental contact.
claims.source_text: It is important to note that NVC in asymptomatic patients is common. … NVC was found in 97.9% of symptomatic and 38.8% of asymptomatic cases … the interpretation of MRI in HFS patients relies on a radiologist or neurosurgeon being familiar with the anatomical details of the facial nerve root. In our experience, initial MRI reports may often overlook the compression at the attached or cisternal segments of the facial nerve, or inaccurately implicate an incidental neurovascular contact.
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **HFS is not life-limiting, and many people choose no procedure;** treatment is for symptoms that distress or reduce quality of life. In one cohort followed for an average of 12 years without treatment, 41.3% were in remission.
claims.source_text: It is important to note that although HFS may produce cosmetic and task-disruptive symptoms, it is still not a life-limiting condition and many patients subsequently choose non-operative management, avoiding surgical interventions that carry small but significant risks. … However, for patients who find the symptoms sufficiently distressing to impact on quality of life, pharmacological or surgical treatments may be sought … a more recent study involving 104 HFS patients with an average follow-up period of 12 years showed that 41.3% of patients were in remission
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Botulinum toxin A is the mainstay for HFS:** it helps most patients (reported efficacy 73 to 98.4%), is used in up to 90%, and keeps working for up to 10 years. Ptosis and facial weakness are the commonest side effects, usually mild and short-lived.
claims.source_text: Botulinum toxin A, continues to produce a significant improvement in symptoms in the majority of patients (efficacy ranging from 73 to 98.4%) … A recent study has therefore implied that it is used in up to 90% of HFS patients … Adverse effects are sometimes reported, with a recent study suggesting that ptosis and facial weakness are the most commonly observed, although these are generally mild and transient if present … it continues to be effective for up to 10 years after its initial commencement in HFS patients
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Toxin resistance is rare at the low doses used in HFS,** but the effect wears off, so injections are repeated every 3 to 6 months by a clinician skilled in choosing doses and target muscles.
claims.source_text: Immunoresistance to botulinum toxin remains rare due to the low dosages often utilized for HFS. However, the ultimate wearing off from the effect still requires patients to attend the clinic on a 3- to 6-monthly basis … The botulinum toxin injections also necessitate appropriately skilled and knowledgeable clinicians to select the optimum dosages and precisely identify the target muscles
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Oral drugs help only a small minority,** mostly on case-report evidence. Carbamazepine, baclofen, pizotifen and clonazepam often cause drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia or weakness in older people; gabapentin and levetiracetam may be better tolerated.
claims.source_text: Oral medications remain a commonly trialed method of treatment for HFS patients, particularly for those who are deemed unsuitable or unkeen to try botulinum toxin or surgical intervention, although the clinical benefit is only observed in a small minority of individuals … the evidence for many of these medications is often based on isolated case reports … Several medications (e.g. carbamazepine, baclofen, pizotifen and clonazepam) also produce unwanted side effects especially in the elderly population, such as somnolence, dizziness, ataxia and weakness. However, gabapentin and levetiracetam may be better tolerated
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Microvascular decompression (MVD) is the only potentially curative treatment,** helping up to 90% of those operated on, yet in some groups only about 10% are referred, after delays of up to 5 years. Tell suitable patients about it and refer in good time.
claims.source_text: Microvascular decompression (MVD) remains the only potential curative treatment for HFS, producing a significant benefit in up to 90% of patients who undergo an operation … only 10% of HFS patients are ultimately referred for MVD [], with a mean delay from diagnosis to surgery of up to 5 years … It is, therefore, essential that clinicians are aware of this highly efficacious treatment option for HFS patients and refer them in timely fashion.
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **After MVD the benefit may be delayed** (in up to 30% of cases, usually about 30 days, occasionally up to a year). Previous botulinum toxin does not worsen surgical results. Up to 9% need a second operation, which works less often and has more complications (nervous system lesions 10.6% after a first operation, 20.7% after revision).
claims.source_text: It is increasingly recognized that there may be a time delay before the effects of MVD are fully noticed (in up to 30% of cases), amounting to approximately 30 days in the majority of patients but can be up to a year in a minority … A very recent study suggested that the use of botulinum toxin as a treatment pre-operatively does not significantly alter surgical outcomes … suggesting that up to 9% of patients may require a re-operation … Re-operations were also shown to be associated with a greater number of complications than a first procedure, with nervous system lesions shown to potentially rise in likelihood from 10.6% with the initial surgery to 20.7% following a revision.
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Other options rest on case reports:** pulsed radiofrequency ablation gives only short-lived relief and often a disfiguring facial palsy; electroacupuncture helped one patient temporarily.
claims.source_text: Further treatments that have previously been suggested for HFS, typically in the form of isolated case reports, include pulse radiofrequency ablation … However, a recent study showed the durability of this intervention is very short and that it also resulted in high rates of disfiguring facial paresis … Electroacupuncture (2 Hz and ~ 1-2 mA intensity used for two periods over 30 weeks) was also attempted in a recent case report, leading to reduced Jankovic Rating and visual analogue scale scores in an HFS patient, although symptoms gradually reappeared at the 6-month follow-up
claims.locator: Jesuthasan A, Natalwala A, Davagnanam I, Saifee T, Zrinzo L (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, UCLH, London), Journal of Neurology 272:502, doi 10.1007/s00415-025-13220-y (narrative review), 'Hemifacial spasm: an update on pathophysiology, investigations and management', published 10 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12245930/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Standard dilution:** 2.5 ml of 0.9% saline per 100 MU of onabotulinumtoxinA (ONA) or incobotulinumtoxinA (INCO). Inject 0.5 ml (20 MU) per site, or 0.2 ml (4 MU) per site in the face.
claims.source_text: The standard dilution is 2.5 ml 0.9% NaCl/H2O per ONA/INCO 100 MU. The standard volume per injection site is 0.5 ml (20 MU), for facial injections 0.2 ml (4 MU).
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep the dilution constant** for patient safety, except in special indications such as hyperhidrosis.
claims.source_text: Unless for special indications, e.g., treatment of hyperhidrosis, dilutions should not vary to increase patient safety.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Products are not interchangeable unit for unit, except ONA and INCO,** which compare at 1:1. Conversion to abobotulinumtoxinA (ABO) is uncertain (1:2 to 1:5), so ABO was left out of the dosing tables; other conversions remain disputed.
claims.source_text: The potency labelling of ONA and INCO may be compared with a conversion factor of 1:1 (Dressler et al., ). Conversion factors between ONA/INCO and other BT drugs are still controversial. … With uncertain conversion factors ranging from 1:2 to 1:5 between the potency labelling of ONA/INCO and ABO, we found it unsafe to include ABO.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Drugs of the same toxin type behave similarly;** INCO, which lacks complexing proteins, has lower antigenicity.
claims.source_text: BT drugs based on different BT types show considerable differences, whereas BT drugs based on the same BT type are very similar. The effects of different excipients including the use of human serum albumin, gelatine and polysorbate are controversially discussed. The lack of complexing proteins and the particular manufacturing process used in INCO has reduced antigenicity.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Storage:** unreconstituted toxin keeps a long time, and only INCO can be stored and shipped at room temperature. Use reconstituted toxin within 24 h, although INCO data suggest it stays stable for at least 1 year.
claims.source_text: Unreconstituted BT drugs have very long shelf lives. Most BT drugs require temperature restrictions. Only INCO may be stored and transported at room temperature. Reconstituted BT drugs should be used within 24 h. Recently published INCO data, however, indicate a stability of at least 1 year
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Injection intervals:** traditionally not less than 12 weeks. INCO has been given at shorter intervals, down to 6 weeks, without toxic or immune complications ('short interval therapy').
claims.source_text: Originally, interinjection intervals were recommended to be not less than 12 weeks. Recent studies indicate that INCO may be applied without toxicological or immunological complications at intervals of less than 12 weeks (Dressler et al ), thus establishing the 'BT short interval therapy'. Interinjection intervals may be as short as 6 weeks
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Total dose per session:** product registrations usually cap it at about 300–400 MU; high-dose studies found INCO totals up to 1250 MU safe, reached by treating more muscles rather than giving more per muscle.
claims.source_text: Registration documents usually recommend maximal total BT doses in the region of 300-400 MU. Recent studies introducing the BT high dose therapy, however, demonstrate the toxicological and immunological safety of maximal total INCO doses of up to 1250 MU, thus establishing the 'BT high dose therapy' ((Dressler et al. ; Wissel et al. ). Note that these doses originate from an increase in the number of target muscles rather than from excessive BT dosing in individual target muscles.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **These doses reflect a centre with few cost or legal limits** that routinely varied registered doses, intervals and contraindications with permission for off-label use.
claims.source_text: The reference centre is able to perform BT therapy with a minimum of economic and legal restrictions. It is thus able to exploit BT therapy's maximum benefit. For all patients treated, BT therapy is free of costs. Regulatory recommendations on target muscle selection and dosing, total doses, inter-injection intervals and contraindications are modified wherever necessary. Permission to perform quantitative and qualitative off-label use was generally granted.
claims.locator: IAB Interdisciplinary Working Group for Movement Disorders (Dressler D, Altavista MC, Altenmueller E, Bhidayasiri R, et al.), Journal of Neural Transmission vol 128, doi 10.1007/s00702-021-02312-4, 'Consensus guidelines for botulinum toxin therapy: general algorithms and dosing tables for dystonia and spasticity', published 26 February 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7969540/, retrieved 2026-09-23
